seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 336 HTS Chapter 28 lines — uranium, ammonia, alumina, acids, caustic soda, silicon and polysilicon, lithium carbonate, rare-earth compounds, iodine and more. Base rates, the 2026 Section 301 rates and the 90 exempt subheadings, China's 25–50%, and the antidumping orders on chemicals.

overview.intro:
Chapter 28 covers inorganic chemicals and the compounds of precious metals, rare-earth metals, radioactive elements and isotopes: chlorine and iodine, industrial gases, silicon and polysilicon, sulfuric, phosphoric and hydrochloric acid, ammonia, caustic soda, alumina, metal oxides, salts such as carbonates, sulfates and phosphates, rare-earth compounds, and uranium. Base rates are low: 103 of the 336 tariff lines are Free and none is above 5.5%. The U.S. imported **$19.38B** of these goods in 2025; **uranium** (heading 2844) alone was $6.97B, followed by alumina ($1.30B) and ammonia ($1.25B).

What decides the duty today is the country and the exact subheading. The **2026 Section 301 tariffs** add 10% or 12.5% on goods of 60 economies, but **90 subheadings (134 lines)** — uranium, ammonia, sulfuric acid, alumina, polysilicon, lithium carbonate, rare-earth compounds, cobalt, antimony and many other critical-mineral chemicals — are exempt under U.S. note 52(b). USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico are exempt too. China pays its List 3 duty of 25% on top (37.5% in total on most lines), and Chinese polysilicon 50%. Several chemicals also carry **antidumping or countervailing duties**, and many carry the **Superfund chemical excise tax** — neither is included in the tariff calculator.

productGroups.label: Chlorine, iodine, fluorine and bromine
productGroups.blurb: Chlorine (Free), iodine (Free), fluorine (3.7%) and bromine (5.5%). Iodine comes mainly from Chile, chlorine from Canada. Tariffs: 1 of 4 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Sublimed, precipitated and colloidal sulfur
productGroups.blurb: Sulfur that has been sublimed (flowers of sulfur), precipitated or made colloidal. Crude and other sulfur is heading 2503. Tariffs: exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Carbon black and other carbon
productGroups.blurb: Carbon black (rubber and pigment grades) and other forms of carbon not elsewhere specified. Activated carbon is heading 3802 and artificial graphite 3801. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply.

productGroups.label: Hydrogen, helium, argon, nitrogen, oxygen, silicon and other nonmetals
productGroups.blurb: Hydrogen, argon, helium, neon and other rare gases, nitrogen, oxygen, boron, tellurium, polysilicon (99.99% silicon or more), silicon metal, phosphorus, arsenic and selenium. Tariffs: 10 of 16 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 1 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)). Silicon metal (2804.69) from ten countries is under antidumping or countervailing duty orders; polysilicon is not.

productGroups.label: Sodium, calcium, lithium and rare-earth metals; mercury
productGroups.blurb: Sodium, potassium, lithium and other alkali metals, calcium and strontium, rare-earth metals (lanthanum, cerium, praseodymium, neodymium and others), scandium, yttrium and mercury. Tariffs: 10 of 13 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Hydrochloric acid and chlorosulfuric acid
productGroups.blurb: Hydrogen chloride (hydrochloric acid, muriatic acid), Free, and chlorosulfuric acid (4.2%). Hydrochloric acid is a DEA List II chemical. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply; 1 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Sulfuric acid and oleum
productGroups.blurb: Sulfuric acid and oleum (fuming sulfuric acid): one line, Free. Sulfuric acid is a DEA List II chemical. Most imports come from Canada and Mexico. Tariffs: exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Nitric acid and sulfonitric acids
productGroups.blurb: Nitric acid and sulfonitric acids (mixed acid): Free. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply.

productGroups.label: Phosphoric acid and phosphorus pentoxide
productGroups.blurb: Phosphoric acid (food, technical and fertilizer grades), polyphosphoric acids and diphosphorus pentaoxide: all Free. Mexico, Belgium, Morocco and Israel are the main suppliers. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply; 4 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Boric acid and oxides of boron
productGroups.blurb: Boric acid and boron oxides: one line at 1.5%. Türkiye is the main supplier. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariff applies.

productGroups.label: Hydrofluoric acid, silicon dioxide and other inorganic acids
productGroups.blurb: Hydrogen fluoride (hydrofluoric acid), hydrogen cyanide, other inorganic acids, carbon dioxide, silicon dioxide (fumed and precipitated silica, silica gel), sulfur dioxide and other inorganic oxygen compounds of nonmetals. Tariffs: 4 of 13 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 2 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Chlorides and oxychlorides of phosphorus and sulfur
productGroups.blurb: Phosphorus trichloride and oxychloride, phosphorus pentachloride, sulfur chlorides, thionyl chloride, carbonyl dichloride (phosgene), boron trifluoride and other halides of nonmetals. Tariffs: 2 of 11 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 1 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Carbon disulfide and other nonmetal sulfides
productGroups.blurb: Carbon disulfide, phosphorus sulfides and other sulfides of nonmetals. Tariffs: 1 of 4 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Ammonia (anhydrous and aqueous)
productGroups.blurb: Anhydrous ammonia and ammonia in water (aqua ammonia): 2 lines, Free. One of the largest items in the chapter by value; Canada and Trinidad and Tobago supply almost all of it. Tariffs: all exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Caustic soda and caustic potash
productGroups.blurb: Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda), solid or in solution (soda lye), potassium hydroxide (caustic potash) and sodium or potassium peroxides. Tariffs: 2 of 5 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 3 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Magnesium hydroxide and peroxide; strontium and barium oxides
productGroups.blurb: Magnesium hydroxide and peroxide and the oxides, hydroxides and peroxides of strontium and barium. Tariffs: all exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Zinc oxide and zinc peroxide
productGroups.blurb: Zinc oxide and zinc peroxide: one line, Free. Mexico and Canada are the main suppliers. Tariffs: exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Aluminum oxide (alumina), corundum and aluminum hydroxide
productGroups.blurb: Artificial corundum (fused alumina), aluminum oxide (smelter-grade and calcined alumina) and aluminum hydroxide. Alumina from Brazil is the largest supply lane in this heading. Tariffs: all exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)). Refined brown aluminum oxide and sol gel alumina abrasive grains from China are under antidumping orders.

productGroups.label: Chromium oxides and hydroxides
productGroups.blurb: Chromium trioxide (chromic acid) and other chromium oxides and hydroxides. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply.

productGroups.label: Manganese oxides
productGroups.blurb: Manganese dioxide (including electrolytic manganese dioxide) and other manganese oxides. Tariffs: 1 of 2 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)). Electrolytic manganese dioxide from China is under an antidumping order.

productGroups.label: Iron oxides and hydroxides; earth colors
productGroups.blurb: Iron oxides and hydroxides (pigment grades and other) and earth colors containing 70% or more combined iron as Fe2O3. Tariffs: all exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Cobalt oxides and hydroxides
productGroups.blurb: Cobalt tetroxide and other cobalt oxides and hydroxides, used in battery cathodes and ceramics: 0.1%. Tariffs: all exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Titanium oxides (titanium dioxide)
productGroups.blurb: Titanium oxides, including titanium dioxide not prepared as a pigment: 5.5%. Titanium dioxide pigments and preparations are heading 3206. Tariffs: exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Lead oxides (litharge, red lead)
productGroups.blurb: Lead monoxide (litharge, massicot), red lead and orange lead, and other lead oxides. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply.

productGroups.label: Lithium hydroxide, hydrazine and other metal oxides and hydroxides
productGroups.blurb: Hydrazine and hydroxylamine, lithium oxide and hydroxide, vanadium, nickel, copper, germanium, molybdenum, antimony, tungsten and other metal oxides, hydroxides and peroxides, and other inorganic bases. Tariffs: 13 of 19 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 1 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Fluorides, fluorosilicates and cryolite
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum, ammonium and sodium fluorides, synthetic cryolite, sodium hexafluoroaluminate, fluorosilicates and other complex fluorine salts. Tariffs: 4 of 8 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Chlorides, oxychlorides, bromides and iodides
productGroups.blurb: Ammonium, calcium, magnesium, aluminum, nickel, zinc, barium, cobalt, copper and other chlorides; chloride oxides and hydroxides; bromides and iodides. Calcium chloride (road deicer) and bromides are the main items. Tariffs: 11 of 24 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 2 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Calcium hypochlorite and other hypochlorites
productGroups.blurb: Commercial calcium hypochlorite (pool chlorine) and other hypochlorites, chlorites and hypobromites. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply. Calcium hypochlorite from China is under antidumping and countervailing duty orders.

productGroups.label: Sodium chlorate, perchlorates and bromates
productGroups.blurb: Sodium chlorate (pulp bleaching), potassium and other chlorates, perchlorates, bromates, iodates and periodates. Canada supplies almost all the sodium chlorate. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply.

productGroups.label: Sulfides and polysulfides
productGroups.blurb: Sodium sulfide, zinc sulfide, cadmium sulfide and other sulfides and polysulfides. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply.

productGroups.label: Dithionites (hydrosulfites) and sulfoxylates
productGroups.blurb: Sodium dithionite (sodium hydrosulfite) and other dithionites and sulfoxylates. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply.

productGroups.label: Sulfites and thiosulfates
productGroups.blurb: Sodium sulfite, sodium metabisulfite and other sulfites, and thiosulfates. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply; 2 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Sulfates, alums and persulfates
productGroups.blurb: Sodium, magnesium, aluminum, nickel, copper, barium, zinc and other sulfates, alums and peroxosulfates (persulfates). Mexico is the main supplier. Tariffs: 8 of 21 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 4 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)). Persulfates from China are under an antidumping order.

productGroups.label: Nitrites and nitrates
productGroups.blurb: Sodium nitrite and potassium nitrite, potassium nitrate and other nitrates (not the fertilizer nitrates of chapter 31). Chile and Israel are the main suppliers. Tariffs: 4 of 7 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 1 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)). Sodium nitrite from China, Germany, India and Russia is under antidumping (and, except Germany, countervailing) duty orders.

productGroups.label: Phosphates, polyphosphates and hypophosphites
productGroups.blurb: Sodium, potassium, calcium and other phosphates, sodium tripolyphosphate (STPP), other polyphosphates, phosphinates and phosphonates. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply; 2 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)). Sodium hexametaphosphate and potassium phosphate salts from China are under antidumping (and countervailing) duty orders.

productGroups.label: Carbonates, including lithium carbonate
productGroups.blurb: Lithium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate, potassium carbonate, calcium carbonate (precipitated), barium and strontium carbonates and other carbonates. Lithium carbonate comes mainly from Argentina and Chile. Tariffs: 7 of 15 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 3 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Cyanides and complex cyanides
productGroups.blurb: Sodium cyanide, potassium cyanide and other cyanides, cyanide oxides and complex cyanides (ferrocyanides, ferricyanides). Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply; 1 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Silicates, including sodium silicate
productGroups.blurb: Sodium silicate (water glass), potassium silicate and other silicates. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply.

productGroups.label: Borates and perborates (refined borax)
productGroups.blurb: Refined borax (sodium tetraborate), anhydrous borax, other borates and perborates. Natural borates are heading 2528. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply.

productGroups.label: Potassium permanganate, chromates, molybdates and other metal-acid salts
productGroups.blurb: Sodium aluminate, sodium and potassium dichromate, potassium permanganate, molybdates, tungstates, ammonium perrhenate, vanadates and other salts of oxometallic acids. Tariffs: 4 of 17 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 1 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)). Potassium permanganate from China and strontium chromate from Austria and France are under antidumping orders.

productGroups.label: Other inorganic salts, including double and complex salts
productGroups.blurb: Double or complex silicates (including synthetic zeolites and aluminosilicates), fulminates, cyanates and thiocyanates, and other salts of inorganic acids. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply; 3 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Precious-metal compounds and colloidal precious metals
productGroups.blurb: Colloidal precious metals, silver nitrate and other silver compounds, gold compounds, platinum-group compounds and amalgams. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply; 3 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Uranium, thorium, plutonium and radioactive isotopes
productGroups.blurb: Natural uranium (oxide, hexafluoride and other compounds), uranium enriched in U-235, depleted uranium, thorium, plutonium, radioactive isotopes for medicine and industry, and spent fuel. The largest heading in the chapter by value. Tariffs: 13 of 23 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 7 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)). Uranium from Russia is under a Commerce suspension agreement and a statutory import ban.

productGroups.label: Stable isotopes, including heavy water
productGroups.blurb: Heavy water (deuterium oxide) and other stable isotopes and their compounds, such as boron-10, lithium-6 and lithium-7 and oxygen-18. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply; 3 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Rare-earth compounds (cerium, lanthanum, yttrium and others)
productGroups.blurb: Cerium compounds and compounds of lanthanum, yttrium, scandium, neodymium and the other rare-earth metals (oxides, chlorides, carbonates and mixtures). China is the main supplier. Tariffs: all exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Hydrogen peroxide
productGroups.blurb: Hydrogen peroxide, whether or not solidified with urea: one line, 3.7%. Canada is the main supplier. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariff applies; 1 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Carbides (silicon carbide, calcium carbide, tungsten carbide)
productGroups.blurb: Calcium carbide, silicon carbide (crude and refined), boron carbide, tungsten carbide and other carbides. Tariffs: 3 of 7 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)).

productGroups.label: Hydrides, nitrides, azides, silicides and borides
productGroups.blurb: Hydrides, nitrides, azides, silicides and borides, such as sodium azide and boron nitride. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply; 1 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

productGroups.label: Mercury compounds
productGroups.blurb: Inorganic and organic compounds of mercury, chemically defined or not. Elemental mercury is heading 2805. Tariffs: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply.

productGroups.label: Phosphides, cyanogen chloride and other inorganic compounds
productGroups.blurb: Phosphides (such as aluminum phosphide), cyanogen chloride, distilled and conductivity water, liquid air and compressed air, amalgams other than of precious metals, and other inorganic compounds. Tariffs: 3 of 5 lines exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); 2 exempt only when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

workedExamples.title: Enriched uranium from France vs. Russia
workedExamples.body: Uranium oxide enriched in U-235 is **Free** under the general rate and on the U.S. note 52(b) exemption list, so it pays no 2026 Section 301 duty from any country: a $10,000,000 cargo from France, the United Kingdom or the Netherlands pays **$0** in duty. Russian enriched uranium is also Free under the column 2 rate, but the **Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act** bans it unless the Department of Energy grants a waiver, and waivers end no later than January 1, 2028. Chinese enriched uranium pays 7.5% (List 4A, 9903.88.15). Every importer also needs the U.S. consignee's NRC license.

workedExamples.title: Anhydrous ammonia from Trinidad and Tobago or Canada
workedExamples.body: Anhydrous ammonia is **Free** and on the note 52(b) exemption list, so ammonia from Trinidad and Tobago, Canada or Algeria pays no customs duty. Chinese ammonia pays 25% (List 3). The importer that sells or uses the ammonia owes the **Superfund chemical excise tax** of **$5.28 per ton** (26 U.S.C. 4661) — $52,800 on 10,000 tons — unless it goes into fertilizer or animal feed (26 U.S.C. 4662(b)). The tax is filed with the IRS on Form 6627, not paid to CBP.

workedExamples.title: Lithium carbonate from Argentina, Chile and China
workedExamples.body: Lithium carbonate carries a **3.7%** base rate and is on the note 52(b) exemption list. From Argentina it pays 3.7% ($37,000 on $1,000,000); from Chile it is **Free** with a U.S.–Chile FTA claim; from China it pays **28.7%** (3.7% + 25% List 3, 9903.88.03) — $287,000 on the same $1,000,000. EU goods pay the 3.7% base rate only, because the EU's 10% minimum does not apply to exempt subheadings.

workedExamples.title: Polysilicon from China and Germany — and the December 2026 minimum price
workedExamples.body: Silicon of at least 99.99% purity (polysilicon) is **Free** and on the note 52(b) exemption list. Chinese polysilicon pays **50%** under the 2024 Section 301 four-year review (9903.91.05); German, Malaysian or Norwegian polysilicon pays nothing. From **December 4, 2026**, Proclamation 11052 adds a Section 232 minimum import price of **$21/kg** (heading 9903.45.33): an importer that does not document a first sale at or above $21/kg pays a specific duty of $21/kg, and one that does pays the difference between the entered value and $21/kg if the entered value is lower.

workedExamples.title: Rare-earth oxides from China
workedExamples.body: Rare-earth compounds are on the note 52(b) exemption list and are **not on any China Section 301 list**, so Chinese rare-earth oxides pay only their base rate: 3.7% on most rare-earth compounds of 2846.90.80, Free on lanthanum, yttrium and scandium compounds of 2846.90.20 and 2846.90.40, and 5.5% on cerium compounds (2846.10). No Section 232 tariff applies: Proclamation 11001 (January 14, 2026) chose negotiations for processed critical minerals instead of tariffs.

**Note 1.** Except where the context otherwise requires, the headings of this chapter apply only to: (a) separate chemical elements and separate chemically defined compounds, whether or not containing impurities; (b) the products mentioned in (a) above dissolved in water; (c) the products mentioned in (a) above dissolved in other solvents provided that the solution constitutes a normal and necessary method of putting up these products adopted solely for reasons of safety or for transport and that the solvent does not render the product particularly suitable for specific use rather than for general use; (d) the products mentioned in (a), (b) or (c) above with an added stabilizer (including an anticaking agent) necessary for their preservation or transport; (e) the products mentioned in (a), (b), (c) or (d) above with an added antidusting agent or a coloring substance added to facilitate their identification or for safety reasons, provided that the additions do not render the product particularly suitable for specific use rather than for general use.

**Note 2.** In addition to dithionites and sulfoxylates, stabilized with organic substances (heading 2831), carbonates and peroxocarbonates of inorganic bases (heading 2836), cyanides, cyanide oxides and complex cyanides of inorganic bases (heading 2837), fulminates, cyanates and thiocyanates, of inorganic bases (heading 2842), organic products included in headings 2843 to 2846 and 2852 and carbides (heading 2849), only the following compounds of carbon are to be classified in this chapter: (a) oxides of carbon, hydrogen cyanide and fulminic, isocyanic, thiocyanic and other simple or complex cyanogen acids (heading 2811); (b) halide oxides of carbon (heading 2812); (c) carbon disulfide (heading 2813); (d) thiocarbonates, selenocarbonates, tellurocarbonates, selenocyanates, tellurocyanates, tetrathiocyanatodiamminochromates (reineckates) and other complex cyanates, of inorganic bases (heading 2842); (e) hydrogen peroxide, solidified with urea (heading 2847), carbon oxysulfide, thiocarbonyl halides, cyanogen, cyanogen halides and cyanamide and its metal derivatives (heading 2853) other than calcium cyanamide, whether or not pure (chapter 31).

**Note 3.** Subject to the provisions of note 1 to section VI, this chapter does not cover: (a) sodium chloride or magnesium oxide, whether or not pure, or other products of section V; (b) organo-inorganic compounds other than those mentioned in note 2 above; (c) products mentioned in note 2, 3, 4 or 5 to chapter 31; (d) inorganic products of a kind used as luminophores, of heading 3206; glass frit and other glass in the form of powder, granules or flakes, of heading 3207; (e) artificial graphite (heading 3801); products put up as charges for fire-extinguishers or put up in fire-extinguishing grenades, of heading 3813; ink removers put up in packings for retail sale, of heading 3824; cultured crystals (other than optical elements) weighing not less than 2.5 g each, of the halides of the alkali or alkaline-earth metals, of heading 3824; (f) precious or semiprecious stones (natural, synthetic or reconstructed) or dust or powder of such stones (headings 7102 to 7105), or precious metals or precious metal alloys of chapter 71; (g) the metals, whether or not pure, metal alloys or cermets, including sintered metal carbides (metal carbides sintered with a metal), of section XV; or (h) optical elements, for example, of the halides of the alkali or alkaline-earth metals (heading 9001).

**Note 4.** Chemically defined complex acids consisting of a nonmetal acid of subchapter II and a metal acid of subchapter IV are to be classified in heading 2811.

**Note 5.** Headings 2826 to 2842 apply only to metal or ammonium salts or peroxysalts. Except where the context otherwise requires, double or complex salts are to be classified in heading 2842.

**Note 6.** Heading 2844 applies only to: (a) technetium (atomic No. 43), promethium (atomic No. 61), polonium (atomic No. 84) and all elements with an atomic number greater than 84; (b) natural or artificial radioactive isotopes (including those of the precious metals or of the base metals of sections XIV and XV), whether or not mixed together; (c) compounds, inorganic or organic, of these elements or isotopes, whether or not chemically defined, whether or not mixed together; (d) alloys, dispersions (including cermets), ceramic products and mixtures containing these elements or isotopes or inorganic or organic compounds thereof and having a specific radioactivity exceeding 74 becquerels per gram (0.002 microcurie per gram); (e) spent (irradiated) fuel elements (cartridges) of nuclear reactors; (f) radioactive residues whether or not usable. The term "isotopes", for the purposes of this note and of the wording of headings 2844 and 2845, refers to: (i) individual nuclides, excluding, however, those existing in nature in the monoisotopic state; (ii) mixtures of isotopes of one and the same element, enriched in one or several of the said isotopes, that is, elements of which the natural isotopic composition has been artificially modified.

**Note 7.** Heading 2853 includes copper phosphide (phosphor copper) containing more than 15 percent by weight of phosphorus.

**Note 8.** Chemical elements (for example, silicon and selenium) doped for use in electronics are to be classified in this chapter, provided that they are in forms unworked as drawn, or in the form of cylinders or rods. When cut in the form of discs, wafers or similar forms, they fall in heading 3818.

**Subheading note 1.** For the purposes of subheading 2852.10, the expression "chemically defined" means all organic or inorganic compounds of mercury meeting the requirements of paragraphs (a) to (e) of note 1 to chapter 28 or paragraphs (a) to (h) of note 1 to chapter 29.

**Statistical note 1.** For the purposes of heading 2804, the term "m3" (cubic meter) means a standard cubic meter measured at 21°C at 760 mm (1013 millibars) pressure.

seo.shortDescription: What changed for inorganic chemical imports since January 2025: the IEEPA duties and their end, the 2026 Section 122 surcharge, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs and their 90 exempt subheadings, China's polysilicon and critical-mineral rates, the Section 232 polysilicon minimum price and the antidumping orders — with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). No Chapter 28 base rate changed; nine statistical lines were added to split existing subheadings.

The extra duties changed a lot. In 2025, non-USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico paid IEEPA duties (10% for Canadian uranium and critical minerals) and goods of most other countries the reciprocal tariff — except 86 Chapter 28 subheadings, mainly critical minerals and energy goods. Those duties **ended on February 24, 2026**; the 10% Section 122 surcharge that followed ran until July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** the **2026 Section 301 tariffs** apply 10% or 12.5% to goods of 60 economies, with 90 Chapter 28 subheadings exempt (U.S. note 52(b)) and USMCA goods exempt. China pays its 2018–2019 list duties on top, and since the 2024 review 25% on certain critical minerals and 50% on polysilicon.

Coming next: a **Section 232 minimum import price of $21/kg on polysilicon** from December 4, 2026. Antidumping or countervailing duty orders cover **silicon metal** from China, Russia, Angola, Laos, Australia, Norway, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iceland, Malaysia and Kazakhstan (new orders on four of them in 2026), **potassium permanganate**, **sodium nitrite**, calcium hypochlorite, persulfates, electrolytic manganese dioxide and several phosphates from China, and **uranium from Russia** is under a suspension agreement. Antidumping and countervailing duties are set by the Commerce Department and are **not included in the tariff calculator**.

For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 28 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 336 Chapter 28 tariff lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. Nine statistical lines are new, splitting existing subheadings without a rate change: germanium dioxide and zirconium dioxide (2825.60), lithium chloride (2827.39.90), zirconium carbonates (2836.99.50) and selenides and tellurides (2842.90.90).

changes.title: Chromium trioxide from India and Türkiye: Commerce final determinations
changes.detail: Commerce found dumping by Indian (14.44%) and Turkish (40.88%) exporters and subsidies in India (29.35%) on chromium trioxide (2819.10). The ITC's final injury vote is pending; there is no order yet.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), with no exemption list for Chapter 28. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China actions, so they did not terminate on their 2026 anniversaries and remain in effect during the statutory review. The 25% List 3 duty on most Chinese Chapter 28 chemicals continues.

changes.title: Potassium phosphate salts from China: orders likely to continue
changes.detail: In the third sunset review Commerce found that revoking the 2010 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on potassium phosphate salts from China (2835.24, 2835.39.10) would likely lead to dumping of up to 95.40% and a subsidy rate of 109.11%. The ITC's review is still open; the orders stay in force meanwhile.

changes.title: Limits on polysilicon imports before the minimum price starts
changes.detail: A BIS temporary final rule (September 22 – December 3, 2026) lets Commerce bar importers that stockpile polysilicon ahead of December 4, and limits importers registered with CBP on or after August 6, 2026 to 12 kg of polysilicon (2804.61.00) a week unless Commerce grants a waiver.

changes.title: Silicon metal orders on Bosnia, Iceland, Malaysia and Kazakhstan continued
changes.detail: After the first five-year review, Commerce continued the 2021 antidumping orders on silicon metal from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iceland and Malaysia and the countervailing duty order on Kazakhstan.
changes.countries: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iceland, Malaysia, Kazakhstan

changes.title: New antidumping and countervailing duties on silicon metal from Australia and Norway
changes.detail: Commerce issued AD and CVD orders on silicon metal (2804.69.10, 2804.69.50) from Australia and Norway. Cash deposits for all other exporters: Australia 6.16% AD + 32.57% CVD; Norway 2.47% AD + 17.27% CVD. Polysilicon (2804.61) is outside the scope.

changes.title: Section 232 minimum import price on polysilicon from December 4, 2026
changes.detail: Proclamation 11052 (signed August 6, 2026) sets a minimum import price of $21/kg for polysilicon (2804.61.00.00) from December 4, 2026 (new heading 9903.45.33, U.S. note 42). An importer that documents a first U.S. sale at or above $21/kg pays nothing more when the entered value is at least $21/kg, or the shortfall when it is lower; without the documentation the duty is $21/kg. It applies in addition to the Section 301 duties. Ingots and wafers (3818) and solar cells and modules (8541) also get a 15% duty.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies take effect
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on goods of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), on top of the base rate, including China, Japan, South Korea, India, Israel, Chile, Trinidad and Tobago, the EU (10% in total) and non-USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico. 90 Chapter 28 subheadings are exempt under U.S. note 52(b) (9903.05.86) and 41 more when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)); the other 202 of 336 lines are covered.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 10% Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) ended after its 150 days on July 23, 2026; the 2026 Section 301 tariffs took over the next day.

changes.title: 25% Section 301 tariff on Brazil takes effect
changes.detail: 25% on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01), on top of the base rate and the 12.5% 2026 duty. 87 Chapter 28 subheadings are exempt under U.S. note 50(a)(ii) (9903.05.03), including alumina, silicon metal, uranium and rare-earth compounds; 45 more when for pharmaceutical use (note 50(a)(v)).

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply — and still lift the 2026 Section 301 duty on Canadian and Mexican goods.

changes.title: No case on lithium hexafluorophosphate from China
changes.detail: The antidumping and countervailing duty petitions on lithium hexafluorophosphate from China (2826.90.90) were withdrawn on April 14, 2026, before Commerce initiated, and the ITC discontinued its investigations.

changes.title: New antidumping and countervailing duties on silicon metal from Angola and Laos
changes.detail: Commerce issued AD orders on silicon metal from Angola (68.45% for all other exporters) and Laos (94.44%) and a CVD order on Laos (69.10%). The ITC found imports from Thailand negligible, so there is no order on Thailand.

changes.title: USTR asks for comments on a critical-minerals trade agreement
changes.detail: Following Proclamation 11001, USTR requested public comments on the design of a plurilateral agreement on trade in critical minerals, including price floors and other measures. No tariff has resulted.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico were exempt, and so were the same 86 Chapter 28 subheadings as under the reciprocal tariff (9903.03.03), including uranium, rare-earth compounds, polysilicon and lithium carbonate; ammonia, sulfuric acid, caustic soda and chlorine paid.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24.

changes.title: Antidumping order on Russian silicon metal continued
changes.detail: Commerce continued the 2003 antidumping order on silicon metal from Russia after the fourth five-year review. The order on silicon metal from China (1991) was continued in November 2023.

changes.title: Section 232 on processed critical minerals: negotiations, no tariff
changes.detail: Proclamation 11001 agreed with Commerce that imports of processed critical minerals and their derivative products threaten national security, but directed Commerce and USTR to negotiate agreements (considering price floors) instead of imposing tariffs. No Section 232 duty applies to rare-earth, lithium, cobalt or other Chapter 28 critical-mineral compounds.

changes.title: China IEEPA fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14357 lowered the IEEPA duty on products of China from 20% to 10% from November 10, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Antidumping order on barium carbonate from China revoked
changes.detail: Commerce revoked the 2003 antidumping order on barium carbonate from China (2836.60) at its sunset review, effective August 20, 2025, because no domestic party took part. A year earlier (November 5, 2024) the orders on barium chloride from China and India (2827.39.45) were revoked at the petitioner's request.

changes.title: Antidumping and countervailing duties on sol gel alumina abrasive grains from China
changes.detail: Commerce issued AD (China-wide 88.32%) and CVD (165.05% for all others) orders on sol gel alumina-based ceramic abrasive grains from China, entered mainly under 2818.10.20 and also under 2818.20 and 2818.30.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff raised to country-specific rates
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025 — for example 15% for Japan, South Korea, Israel and Trinidad and Tobago, and 15% in total for the EU. The exempt subheadings stayed exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Extra 40% IEEPA duty on goods of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added 40% on goods of Brazil, on top of the reciprocal tariff, for goods entered from August 6, 2025, with an annex of exempt products. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada IEEPA duty raised to 35% on non-USMCA goods
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on Canadian goods not entered under USMCA from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10); Canadian energy, uranium and critical minerals stayed at 10% (9903.01.13). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on most Chapter 28 goods
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico, from April 5, 2025. 86 Chapter 28 subheadings — among them uranium, polysilicon, rare-earth metals and compounds, lithium carbonate and hydroxide, cobalt, antimony, manganese and titanium oxides and iodine — are on the exemption list printed in the schedule (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)(a)); ammonia, sulfuric acid, caustic soda, chlorine and most salts paid. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China IEEPA fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14228 raised the IEEPA duty on products of China (9903.01.20) from 10% to 20%, on top of the Section 301 duties. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada, Mexico and China
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01), in force from March 4, 2025, with 10% for Canadian energy resources, uranium and critical minerals (9903.01.13); +10% on goods of China (9903.01.20) from February 4, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: 50% Section 301 tariff on Chinese polysilicon
changes.detail: As announced in the 2024 four-year review, polysilicon of China (2804.61) pays 50% from January 1, 2025 (9903.91.05, U.S. note 31(f)), up from 25% under List 3. USTR's December 2025 semiconductor action schedules a further increase for June 23, 2027, in an amount not yet announced.

changes.title: 25% Section 301 tariff on Chinese critical minerals
changes.detail: The 2024 four-year review moved seven Chapter 28 subheadings — among them tungstates, a tungsten oxide line, radioactive isotopes (2844.41–2844.44) and a carbide line — to heading 9903.91.01 at 25% from September 27, 2024 (U.S. note 31(b)).

changes.title: Ban on Russian low-enriched uranium takes effect
changes.detail: The Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act (Public Law 118-62, signed May 13, 2024) bans imports of unirradiated low-enriched uranium produced in Russia or by a Russian entity from August 11, 2024, with DOE waivers capped each year and ending no later than January 1, 2028. The NRC applies it to natural uranium too. This is an import ban, not a tariff.

changes.title: 35% in lieu of column 2 on certain Russian chemicals
changes.detail: Proclamation 10420 set a 35% rate in place of the column 2 rate for listed products of Russia (9903.90.08, U.S. note 30), and Proclamation 10523 added more from April 1, 2023, including carbon black (2803), selenium (2804.90), calcium (2805.12) and rare-earth compounds (2846.90). 56 Chapter 28 subheadings (75 lines) are covered. Still in force.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 28 goods were **$19.38B in 2025**, +2.3% from $18.95B in 2024, almost level with the 2022 peak of $19.42B and up from $10.74B in 2020. **Uranium** (heading 2844) is the largest item by far: $6.97B (36%), mostly enriched uranium ($4.38B) and natural uranium compounds such as uranium hexafluoride ($1.87B), plus radioactive isotopes for medicine and industry ($715M). It comes from **France** ($1.71B), the **United Kingdom** ($1.36B), **Canada** ($1.16B), **Russia** ($1.06B), the Netherlands ($750M), Germany ($442M) and Kazakhstan ($215M). That is why France and the UK rank second and third among all suppliers.

**Alumina and aluminum hydroxide** (heading 2818) rose to $1.30B from $1.06B, $635M of it from Brazil. **Ammonia** was $1.25B: $761M from Canada and $399M from Trinidad and Tobago. Silicon metal ($487M) is the largest item of heading 2804, where Brazil and Canada are the top suppliers; polysilicon imports rose to $190M from $103M. **Antimony oxides** more than doubled to $529M. Other large lines are sulfuric acid ($435M, mostly from Canada), carbon black ($421M), phosphoric acid ($331M), iodine ($199M, $175M from Chile), lithium carbonate ($163M, from Argentina and Chile) and rare-earth compounds ($201M, $109M from China).

Canada is the largest supplier overall ($3.74B, 19%), shipping uranium, ammonia, sulfuric acid and sodium chlorate that mostly enter Free. Imports from China fell to $1.39B from $1.88B. The 2025 figures predate the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, which exempt uranium, ammonia, alumina and most critical-mineral chemicals. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

seo.shortDescription: The total U.S. tariff on inorganic chemicals by country and product group: Free with USMCA for Canada and Mexico, 10% for the EU and the UK, 12.5% for Japan and South Korea, up to 37.5% plus base for China and Brazil — with the 90 exempt subheadings (uranium, ammonia, alumina, critical minerals) explained.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. Base rates in this chapter are 0–5.5%, so the total is mainly the **2026 Section 301 rate** of the country: 10% or 12.5%, or a 10% (EU) or 12.5% (Japan, South Korea) total in place of a lower base rate.

Two things change the answer. A **USMCA claim** removes the 10% duty on Canadian and Mexican goods — compare the two Canada and Mexico columns. And 90 subheadings (uranium, ammonia, sulfuric acid, alumina, polysilicon, lithium carbonate, rare-earth compounds and most critical-mineral chemicals) are **exempt** under U.S. note 52(b), so they pay only the base rate from almost every country. China pays its List 3 duty on top (37.5% plus base on most lines), Brazil a further 25%. The table does **not** include antidumping or countervailing duties, the Superfund chemical excise tax or the December 2026 Section 232 polysilicon minimum price.

assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-12, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.

Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; KR for South Korea; CL for Chile; IL for Israel. GSP (A, A+) has lapsed and is not applied. Other preferences are not applied.
Conditional relief is not applied (it needs the importer's confirmation): 9903.05.89 (Section 301), 9903.05.06 (Section 301), 9903.88.69 (Section 301).
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026. Neither is applied.

Exemption lists checked in the 2026 Revision 21: U.S. note 52(b) (90 Chapter 28 subheadings exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties), note 52(e) (41 more when for pharmaceutical use, not applied), note 50(a)(ii) (87 exempt from the Brazil duty), notes 20(b), 20(f) and 20(s) (China Lists 1, 3 and 4A), note 31 (China 2024 review) and note 30 (Russia). Not included: antidumping and countervailing duties on Chapter 28 chemicals, the Superfund chemical excise tax (an IRS tax, not a customs duty), the Section 232 polysilicon minimum import price from December 4, 2026, the ban on Russian low-enriched uranium, and entry rules (TSCA certification, DEA listed chemicals, NRC licenses).

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 28: Inorganic Chemicals, Rare-Earth, Precious-Metal & Radioactive Compounds — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Inorganic Chemicals: TSCA, DEA, NRC Rules and Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 28) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 28 line — TSCA import certification, DEA listed chemicals (iodine, phosphorus, permanganate), NRC licenses and the Russian uranium ban, CWC declarations, hazmat, the Superfund chemical tax, antidumping orders — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, exempt subheadings, FTAs, drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Chapter 28 base rates are low (103 of 336 lines Free, none above 5.5%), so the levers that matter are about the **extra duties**: a USMCA claim removes the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian and Mexican goods, the 90 exempt subheadings pay no 2026 Section 301 duty from any country, FTA claims remove the base rate, and drawback can return duties on chemicals that are exported again. Antidumping and countervailing duties and the Superfund chemical excise tax are **not included in the tariff calculator**.

The paperwork depends on the chemical: every shipment needs a TSCA certification; iodine, phosphorus, hydriodic and hypophosphorous acid and the permanganates are DEA listed chemicals; uranium and radioactive isotopes need an NRC-licensed consignee and Russian uranium a DOE waiver; Chemical Weapons Convention chemicals need BIS declarations; mercury imports are reported to EPA; and acids, gases and phosphorus are hazardous materials in transport. Each rule and lever below links to its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on Canadian and Mexican chemicals
levers.saves: 10% of value: the 2026 Section 301 duty on Canada (9903.05.29) and Mexico (9903.05.55) does not apply to goods entered under USMCA (9903.05.93 / 9903.05.94), and the base rate (up to 5.5%) is removed too
levers.appliesTo: The 202 lines not on the note 52(b) list (plus the base rate on any dutiable line), for originating goods of Canada or Mexico
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer with the minimum data elements; it need not follow a prescribed format and CBP can ask for it. Chapter 28 goods usually qualify through a change in tariff classification or a chemical reaction in Canada or Mexico, under the product-specific rules of General Note 11.
levers.caveat: Mixing, dilution or repackaging alone does not confer origin. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(g)–(h)
USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Classify to the exact subheading
levers.saves: 10–12.5% (37.5% for China): the 90 note 52(b) subheadings pay no 2026 Section 301 duty, and rare-earth compounds, alumina (2818.20) and antimony oxides are on no China list
levers.appliesTo: Uranium, ammonia, sulfuric acid, alumina, polysilicon, lithium compounds, rare earths, cobalt, antimony, iron and manganese oxides and the other exempt chemicals
levers.document: A certificate of analysis or specification sheet that supports the subheading: for example polysilicon (99.99% silicon or more, 2804.61, exempt) versus silicon metal (2804.69, not exempt), lithium carbonate (2836.91, exempt) versus other carbonates, or rare-earth compound by predominant metal (2846.90.20 / .40 / .80).
levers.caveat: Classification follows the General Rules of Interpretation and chapter note 1 (separate, chemically defined compounds); it cannot be chosen to save duty. Mixtures and preparations move to chapter 38. When unsure, ask CBP for a binding ruling.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(b)

levers.title: Document pharmaceutical use for the note 52(e) chemicals
levers.saves: 10–12.5%: 41 Chapter 28 subheadings — such as hydrochloric and phosphoric acid, caustic soda and potash, sodium bicarbonate, potassium carbonate, hydrogen peroxide and isotopes — are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty when for use in pharmaceutical applications (9903.05.89); the same for Brazil's 25% (note 50(a)(v))
levers.appliesTo: The 49 lines of the 41 note 52(e) subheadings, when they go into pharmaceutical manufacture
levers.document: Evidence of the pharmaceutical end use (purchase orders or contracts with a drug manufacturer, the grade such as USP or EP) kept to support the claim if CBP asks.
levers.caveat: Industrial-grade goods for other uses pay the duty. The claim does not lift China's List 3 duty.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(e)

levers.title: Compare countries of origin
levers.saves: Up to 12.5 points (more for China): EU and UK goods pay 10%, Japan and South Korea 12.5% in total, USMCA goods and countries outside the 60 Section 301 economies nothing; China up to 37.5% plus base
levers.appliesTo: The 202 lines not on the note 52(b) list
levers.document: The commercial invoice and a certificate of analysis or manufacturer's declaration showing where the chemical was produced (reacted), not just where it was blended or packed.
levers.caveat: Section 301 duties follow the country of origin, not the shipping country. Antidumping orders follow their own scope and may cover goods processed in a third country.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52

levers.title: Claim an FTA preference on the dutiable lines
levers.saves: The base rate of up to 5.5% on the 233 dutiable lines — for example helium and argon 3.7%, titanium oxides and cerium compounds 5.5%, lithium carbonate 3.7%
levers.appliesTo: Goods of FTA partners such as Australia, Chile, Colombia, Israel, Korea, Morocco, Peru or Singapore, on lines that list their code in the Special column
levers.document: The origin documentation required by the agreement (19 CFR part 10 and the agreement's subpart).
levers.caveat: The Section 301 duty still applies when an FTA rate is claimed (note 52(a)), and Japan, South Korea and the EU pay their 12.5% or 10% total either way on covered lines. GSP has lapsed.

levers.title: Claim drawback on chemicals that are exported again
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, including the Section 301 duties, on imported chemicals that are exported unused or used to make exported goods; a substitute chemical of the same 8-digit subheading can be used
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191); substitution claims under 19 U.S.C. 1313(b) or (j)(2) within 5 years.
levers.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refundable as drawback (19 CFR 191.3).

levers.title: Use the Superfund chemical tax exemptions
levers.saves: The excise tax per ton (e.g. $5.28 on ammonia, $0.52 on sulfuric acid, $0.48 on nitric acid) when the chemical goes into fertilizer or animal feed, is exported, or is used to make another taxable chemical
levers.appliesTo: Taxable chemicals of 26 U.S.C. 4661 imported and sold or used in the United States — ammonia, chlorine, acids, caustic soda and potash, phosphorus, bromine, arsenic, mercury and others
levers.document: Exemption certificates and records under the IRS regulations; the tax and any credit are reported on Form 6627 with Form 720.
levers.caveat: This is an IRS excise tax, not a customs duty; it is not shown in the tariff calculator.

levers.title: Check the scope of antidumping and countervailing duty orders
levers.saves: The AD/CVD cash deposit — 2% to over 200% of value — when the product or its producer is outside the order or has its own lower rate
levers.appliesTo: Silicon metal, potassium permanganate, sodium nitrite, calcium hypochlorite, persulfates, electrolytic manganese dioxide, certain phosphates and alumina abrasives from the countries named in each order
levers.document: The order's written scope decides, not the HTS number: for example polysilicon of 99.99% silicon or more (2804.61) is excluded from every silicon metal order. Producers with their own reviewed rate pay that rate instead of the all-others rate. When unsure, request a scope ruling from Commerce.
levers.caveat: Goods inside the scope pay the cash deposit even if entered under another HTS line, and the final duty can be set higher in an administrative review. AD/CVD duties are not refundable as drawback.

rules.title: Every Chapter 28 chemical: TSCA import certification (positive, or negative for a chemical not subject to TSCA) filed before release; without it CBP detains the shipment

Iodine, red and white phosphorus, hydriodic acid, and hypophosphorous acid and its salts (List I): DEA importer registration and a DEA Form 486 import declaration at least 15 days before release (3 business days for regular importers); no threshold except 1.7 kg for hydriodic acid

Potassium and sodium permanganate (List II): DEA Form 486 import declaration at least 15 days before release for shipments of 500 kg or more. Hydrochloric and sulfuric acid are List II chemicals, but their imports are excluded from the declaration rules

Uranium, thorium, plutonium and radioactive isotopes: imported under the NRC general license only when the U.S. consignee holds an NRC or Agreement State license to possess the material; irradiated fuel over 100 kg per shipment and radioactive waste need a specific license (NRC Form 7). Heavy water and deuterium need no NRC import license

Russian uranium: low-enriched uranium produced in Russia or by a Russian entity is banned since August 11, 2024 (NRC also applies the ban to natural uranium). DOE waivers, capped at 464,183 kg in 2026 and 459,083 kg in 2027, end no later than January 1, 2028

citations.label: Public Law 118-62 (Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act)
89 FR 45926 (NRC: effect of the statutory prohibition)

rules.title: Chemical Weapons Convention chemicals: arsenic trichloride (Schedule 2) cannot be imported from countries outside the Convention and needs an annual declaration above 1 t; phosgene, hydrogen cyanide, cyanogen chloride and the phosphorus and sulfur chlorides (Schedule 3) need an annual declaration when imports of one chemical exceed 30 t

Elemental mercury and mercury compounds: importers report quantities and countries of origin to EPA's mercury inventory every three years (reporting year 2027, due July 1, 2028); export of elemental mercury and five mercury compounds is banned

Hazardous materials in transport: for example anhydrous ammonia (UN1005), chlorine (UN1017), sulfuric acid (UN1830), hydrochloric acid (UN1789), caustic soda solution (UN1824), hydrogen peroxide (UN2014/UN2015), nitric acid (UN2031), white phosphorus (UN1381) and mercury (UN2809) need hazmat shipping papers, marking and packaging

Chemicals imported as pesticides (for example boric acid, sodium chlorate, copper sulfate, sulfur or aluminum and zinc phosphide sold as a pesticide): EPA Notice of Arrival before the shipment arrives; otherwise the TSCA certification applies

Superfund chemical excise tax (not a customs duty): due when the importer sells or uses a taxable chemical, e.g. ammonia $5.28, chlorine $5.40, hydrogen fluoride $8.46, phosphorus, arsenic, bromine and mercury $8.90, sulfuric acid $0.52 and caustic soda $0.56 per ton; imported hydrogen peroxide, chromic acid and nickel oxide pay the tax on imported substances. Reported on Form 6627 with Form 720

Polysilicon (2804.61): Section 232 minimum import price of $21/kg from December 4, 2026; until then, new importers registered on or after August 6, 2026 may bring in at most 12 kg a week without a Commerce waiver

Silicon metal (2804.69.10, 2804.69.50) from China, Russia, Angola, Laos, Australia, Norway, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iceland, Malaysia (antidumping) and Kazakhstan, Laos, Australia, Norway (countervailing): cash deposit at entry; polysilicon (2804.61) is excluded (not in the tariff calculator)

Uranium from Russia (2844.10, 2844.20): Commerce suspension agreement on the antidumping investigation, continued in 2023 (export limits instead of a duty), on top of the statutory import ban (not in the tariff calculator)
Potassium permanganate (2841.61) from China: antidumping order since 1984 (not in the tariff calculator)
Sodium nitrite (2834.10.10) from China (AD + CVD), Germany (AD), India (AD + CVD) and Russia (AD + CVD) (not in the tariff calculator)

Calcium hypochlorite (2828.10, AD + CVD), persulfates (2833.40), electrolytic manganese dioxide (2820.10), sodium hexametaphosphate (2835.39.50) and potassium phosphate salts (2835.24, 2835.39.10, AD + CVD) from China (not in the tariff calculator)

Refined brown aluminum oxide (2818.10.20) and sol gel alumina abrasive grains (2818.10.20, also 2818.20 and 2818.30) from China; strontium chromate (2841.50.91) from Austria and France (not in the tariff calculator)

groups.label: Chlorine, iodine, fluorine and bromine

finalConclusion.h1: HTS Chapter 28: Inorganic Chemicals, Rare-Earth, Precious-Metal & Radioactive Compounds — Tariff FAQ

seo.title: Chemical Tariffs FAQ — HTS Chapter 28: Rare Earth, Polysilicon, Uranium & China Chemical Tariffs | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to the most-searched questions on inorganic chemical tariffs: tariffs on chemicals from China, rare-earth and critical-mineral tariffs, the Section 232 polysilicon tariff, uranium tariffs, the Superfund chemical tax and the HTS codes for ammonia, silicon and lithium carbonate.
keywords: are there tariffs on rare earth minerals

finalConclusion.intro: The questions below are the ones people search for most about tariffs on inorganic chemicals, critical minerals and uranium. Each answer is drawn from the official sources on the other pages of this chapter, as of the current tariff schedule (2026 Revision 21).
keyTakeaways: Base rates are low: 103 of 336 Chapter 28 lines are Free and none is above 5.5%; no base rate changed between January 2025 and October 2026.

The 2026 Section 301 tariffs (10% or 12.5%, since July 24, 2026) cover 202 lines, but 90 subheadings — uranium, ammonia, sulfuric acid, alumina, polysilicon, lithium carbonate, rare earths and most critical-mineral chemicals — are exempt, and USMCA goods are exempt.
China pays 25% (List 3) plus 12.5% on most chemicals, 50% on polysilicon and 7.5% on enriched uranium; rare-earth compounds, alumina and antimony oxides from China pay only the base rate.
No Section 232 tariff applies to critical minerals (Proclamation 11001 chose negotiations), but polysilicon gets a $21/kg minimum import price from December 4, 2026.
Russian low-enriched uranium is banned without a DOE waiver, and waivers end by January 1, 2028.
Antidumping and countervailing duties on chemicals such as silicon metal and potassium permanganate, and the Superfund chemical excise tax, come on top and are not in the tariff calculator.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on chemicals from China?
faqs.answer: Most Chinese inorganic chemicals (Chapter 28) pay their base rate (0–5.5%) plus 25% under Section 301 List 3 (9903.88.03) plus 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.31) — 37.5% plus base, for example 37.5% on chlorine. Chemicals on the 2026 exemption list but on List 3, such as ammonia, zinc oxide and lithium carbonate, pay base + 25%. Chinese polysilicon pays 50%, enriched uranium 7.5%, and rare-earth compounds, alumina (2818.20) and antimony oxides only the base rate. Some products, such as potassium permanganate and calcium hypochlorite, also pay antidumping duties. The 2025 IEEPA duties on China ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on rare earth minerals and compounds from China?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on rare earth minerals
us tariff on china rare earth
faqs.answer: Only the base rate. Rare-earth metals (2805.30, 5%) and rare-earth compounds (2846: Free, 3.7% or 5.5%) are not on any China Section 301 list and are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)), so Chinese rare-earth oxides pay 3.7% on most lines and 5.5% on cerium compounds. No Section 232 tariff applies: Proclamation 11001 (January 14, 2026) chose negotiations on processed critical minerals instead. Rare-earth magnets are not in this chapter (heading 8505).

faqs.question: What is the Section 232 tariff on polysilicon?
faqs.answer: Proclamation 11052 (August 6, 2026) sets a minimum import price of $21/kg for polysilicon (2804.61.00.00) from December 4, 2026 (heading 9903.45.33): an importer that does not document a first U.S. sale at or above $21/kg pays $21/kg, and one that does pays the difference when the entered value is below $21/kg. The 15% Section 232 duty applies to polysilicon ingots and wafers (3818) and solar cells and modules (8541), not to polysilicon itself. Today polysilicon is Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, except from China, which pays 50% under Section 301 (9903.91.05).

faqs.question: Are critical minerals exempt from tariffs?
faqs.answer: Largely, yes. The 2026 Section 301 tariffs exempt 90 Chapter 28 subheadings (U.S. note 52(b)), including lithium, cobalt, antimony, manganese, rare-earth, gallium and germanium compounds, polysilicon and uranium. The Section 232 investigation of processed critical minerals ended with Proclamation 11001 (January 14, 2026), which chose negotiations and possible price floors instead of tariffs. China is the exception: most critical-mineral chemicals still pay China's 25% List 3 duty, and seven subheadings such as tungstates pay 25% under the 2024 review.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on uranium?
faqs.answer: No. Natural uranium compounds (2844.10.20) and enriched uranium (2844.20) are Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, so uranium from Canada, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Germany or Kazakhstan pays no duty; uranium metal (2844.10.10) is 5%. Chinese enriched uranium pays 7.5% (List 4A). In 2025, Canadian uranium paid a 10% IEEPA duty when not entered under USMCA; that ended February 24, 2026. The U.S. consignee must hold an NRC license.

faqs.question: Does the U.S. still import uranium from Russia?
searchedAs: does the us still import uranium from russia
does the us import uranium from russia
faqs.answer: Only with a waiver. The Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act bans low-enriched uranium produced in Russia or by a Russian entity from August 11, 2024; the Department of Energy may grant waivers up to 464,183 kg in 2026 and 459,083 kg in 2027, and all waivers end by January 1, 2028. The U.S. still imported $1.06B of Russian uranium and radioactive goods in 2025. Russian uranium is also under a Commerce antidumping suspension agreement. It pays no tariff.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. get its uranium?
searchedAs: where does the us get uranium
where does the us import uranium from
where does the us get enriched uranium
what countries does the us import uranium from
faqs.answer: In 2025 the U.S. imported $6.97B of uranium and other radioactive goods (heading 2844): $4.38B of enriched uranium and $1.87B of natural uranium compounds. The largest suppliers were France ($1.71B), the United Kingdom ($1.36B), Canada ($1.16B), Russia ($1.06B), the Netherlands ($750M), Germany ($442M) and Kazakhstan ($215M).

faqs.question: How do the 2026 U.S. tariffs affect chemical imports?
faqs.answer: For inorganic chemicals the main tariff since July 24, 2026 is the 2026 Section 301 action: 10% or 12.5% on goods of 60 economies (10% in total for the EU, 12.5% in total for Japan and South Korea), on top of base rates of 0–5.5%. It covers 202 of 336 Chapter 28 lines; 90 subheadings are exempt and USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico are exempt. The IEEPA tariffs of 2025 ended February 24, 2026 and the 10% Section 122 surcharge ran until July 23, 2026. Organic chemicals are in Chapter 29.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on chemicals from India?
searchedAs: us tariff on chemicals from india
faqs.answer: Indian inorganic chemicals pay their base rate plus 10% under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.44) — 10% on Indian carbon black, for example — unless the subheading is on the note 52(b) exemption list. Sodium nitrite from India also pays antidumping and countervailing duties, and chromium trioxide from India faces new ones once the ITC votes. The 2025 IEEPA duties on India ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the Superfund chemical excise tax, and which chemicals are taxed?
faqs.answer: It is a federal excise tax (26 U.S.C. 4661), reinstated from July 1, 2022 through 2031, on taxable chemicals sold or used by their manufacturer, producer or importer — not a customs duty. Chapter 28 examples per ton: ammonia $5.28, chlorine $5.40, hydrogen fluoride $8.46, phosphorus, bromine, arsenic and mercury $8.90, lead oxide $8.28, sulfuric acid $0.52, caustic soda $0.56, nitric acid $0.48 and potassium hydroxide $0.44. Imported hydrogen peroxide, chromic acid and nickel oxide pay the tax on imported substances (26 U.S.C. 4671). Ammonia, sulfuric and nitric acid for fertilizer or feed are exempt. It is reported on IRS Form 6627.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for silicon metal and polysilicon, and what duty applies?
faqs.answer: Silicon with at least 99.99% silicon (polysilicon) is 2804.61.00.00: Free, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, 50% for China, and a $21/kg minimum import price from December 4, 2026. Silicon metal is 2804.69.10 (99% to under 99.99% silicon, 5.3%) or 2804.69.50 (under 99%, 5.5%); it is not exempt, so for example Brazil pays 17.8% and China 17.8%, and silicon metal from ten countries also carries antidumping or countervailing duties. Wafers cut from doped silicon are heading 3818.

faqs.question: Which countries face antidumping duties on silicon metal?
faqs.answer: Silicon metal (2804.69) is under antidumping orders on China (since 1991), Russia (2003), Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iceland and Malaysia (2021), Angola and Laos (April 2026) and Australia and Norway (August 2026), and countervailing duty orders on Kazakhstan, Laos, Australia and Norway. Cash deposits for exporters without their own rate range from 2.47% (Norway AD) to 94.44% (Laos AD). Polysilicon (2804.61) is excluded from every order. These duties are not in the tariff calculator.

faqs.question: What is the tariff code for ammonia, and is there a tariff on it?
faqs.answer: Anhydrous ammonia is 2814.10.00.00 and ammonia in water 2814.20.00.00. Both are Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, so ammonia from Canada ($761M in 2025) or Trinidad and Tobago ($399M) pays no customs duty; Chinese ammonia pays 25% (List 3). The importer owes the Superfund chemical excise tax of $5.28 per ton unless the ammonia goes into fertilizer or animal feed. Ammonium nitrate and other ammonium fertilizers are in Chapter 31.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on lithium carbonate and lithium hydroxide?
faqs.answer: Lithium carbonate is 2836.91 and lithium oxide and hydroxide 2825.20, both 3.7% and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs. Argentine lithium carbonate pays 3.7%; Chilean, Australian and Korean goods are Free with an FTA claim; Chinese lithium carbonate pays 28.7% (3.7% + 25% List 3). Lithium-ion batteries are not in this chapter (8507).

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for titanium dioxide?
faqs.answer: Titanium oxides, including titanium dioxide not prepared as a pigment, are 2823.00.00.00 at 5.5%. The line is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, so German TiO2 of this line pays 5.5% (Korean is Free with a KORUS claim); Chinese pays 30.5% (5.5% + 25% List 3). Titanium dioxide pigments and preparations with 80% or more TiO2 are classified in heading 3206, not here.
